native_verses.65:19: I will exult in Jerusalem and be joyful in My people; never again will the sound of weeping or the sound of outcry be heard in her.
native_verses.65:20: There will no longer be an infant there of a few days, nor an elderly man who does not complete his days; for the youth will die at a hundred years old, and the sinner at a hundred years old will be cursed.
native_verses.65:21: They will build houses and live in them, and they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit.
native_verses.65:22: They will not build and another live there; they will not plant and another eat; for like the days of a tree will be the days of My people, and My chosen ones will use to the full the work of their hands.
native_verses.65:23: They will not toil in vain, nor bear children for sudden disaster, because they are the seed of the LORD's blessed ones, and their descendants are with them.
native_verses.65:24: And it will happen that before they call, I will answer, and while they are still speaking, I will listen.
native_verses.65:25: Wolf and lamb will graze together, and the lion will eat straw like cattle; as for the serpent, dust will be its food. They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain," says the LORD.
native_verses.66:1: This is what the LORD says: "The heavens are My throne, and the earth is the footstool for My feet. Where is a house that you would build for Me, and where is a place of My rest?
native_verses.66:2: My hand made all these things, and all these things came into existence," declares the LORD. "Yet to this person I will look: to one who is humble and stricken in spirit, and who trembles at My word.
native_verses.66:3: One who slaughters an ox is like one who strikes down a man; one who sacrifices a lamb, like one who snaps a dog's neck; one who offers up a grain offering, like offering swine's blood; one who offers a memorial of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol. Just as they have chosen their own ways, and their soul takes pleasure in their detestable things,
native_verses.66:4: so I too will choose their afflictions and bring the things they fear upon them; because I called and there was no one answering, I spoke and they did not listen; instead, they did evil in My eyes and chose that in which I took no pleasure."
native_verses.66:5: Listen to the word of the LORD, you who tremble at His word: "Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for the sake of My name, have said, 'May the LORD show His glory, so that we may witness your joy!' Yet they themselves will be shamed."
native_verses.66:6: A sound of tumult from the city, a voice from the temple—the voice of the LORD repaying retribution to His enemies!
native_verses.66:7: Before she writhed in labor, she gave birth; before a birth pang came to her, she delivered a male child.
native_verses.66:8: Who has heard of something like this? Who has seen things like these? Can a land be brought forth in a single day, or can a nation be born at one stroke? For as soon as Zion writhed in labor, she also gave birth to her sons.
native_verses.66:9: "Would I bring to the moment of birth and not cause delivery?" says the LORD. "Or would I, the One who causes delivery, close the womb?" says your God.
native_verses.66:10: Rejoice with Jerusalem and exult in her, all who love her; be joyful with her in joy, all who mourn over her,
native_verses.66:11: so that you may nurse and be filled from the breast of her comfort, so that you may drink deeply and take delight from the abundance of her glory.
native_verses.66:12: For this is what the LORD says: "Look, I am extending peace toward her like a river, and the glory of nations like a rushing stream; and you will nurse, you will be carried at the hip, and you will be bounced upon the knees.
native_verses.66:13: Like a man whose mother comforts him, so I Myself will comfort you, and in Jerusalem you will be comforted.
native_verses.66:14: You will see, and your heart will be joyful, and your bones will sprout like tender grass; the hand of the LORD will become known among His servants, and He will express indignation against His enemies."
native_verses.66:15: For look, the LORD is coming in fire, and His chariots are like the whirlwind, to discharge His anger in fury and His rebuke in flames of fire.
native_verses.66:16: For by fire the LORD is entering into judgment, and by His sword with all flesh; and many will be those struck down by the LORD.
native_verses.66:17: "Those who consecrate themselves and purify themselves for the gardens, behind one in the middle, eating the flesh of swine and the detestable thing and the mouse—together they will come to an end," declares the LORD.
native_verses.66:18: "And I know their deeds and their thoughts; the time is coming to gather all the nations and languages, and they will come and see My glory.
native_verses.66:19: I will place a sign among them and send out survivors from them to the nations—to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the distant coastlands that have not heard of My fame and have not seen My glory—and they will proclaim My glory among the nations.
native_verses.66:20: And they will bring all your brothers out of all the nations as an offering to the LORD—on horses, in chariots, in covered wagons, on mules, and on dromedaries—to My holy mountain Jerusalem," says the LORD, "just as the sons of Israel bring the offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD.
native_verses.66:21: And from among them as well I will take some as priests and as Levites," says the LORD.
native_verses.66:22: "For just as the new heavens and the new earth that I am making will stand before Me," declares the LORD, "so your seed and your name will stand.
native_verses.66:23: And it will come about that from one new moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another, all flesh will come to bow down before Me," says the LORD.
native_verses.66:24: "And they will go out and look upon the corpses of the men who rebelled against Me; for their worm will not die, and their fire will not go out, and they will be a horror to all flesh."

native_notes.1:7: The Masoretic Text repeats zarim ("foreigners") in the final clause ("an overthrow by foreigners"), matching the preceding line; the noun mahpekah ("overthrow") is also the term commonly associated with the destruction of Sodom (cf. v. 9).
native_notes.1:12: The Masoretic vocalization points lera'ot as a Niphal infinitive construct of ra'ah ("to appear") with panai ("My face/presence") as an adverbial accusative, the traditional pious pointing of the idiom for appearing at the sanctuary.
native_notes.1:17: The Piel imperative ashru ("set straight/correct") governs the rare noun chamos, which is understood either as an active agent ("oppressor/ruthless one") or passively as "the oppressed" (yielding "relieve the oppressed").
native_notes.1:20: Hebrew creates a sharp wordplay with v. 19 using the same verb akal ("eat/devour"): Qal active to'kelu ("you will eat") in v. 19 is answered by Pual passive te'ukkelu ("you will be devoured") with instrumental cherev ("by the sword") in v. 20.
native_notes.1:29: The Masoretic Text shifts mid-sentence from third-person plural ("they will be ashamed") to second-person plural ("you desired ... you will be disgraced ... you chose"), a classic prophetic shift of person retained here.
native_notes.2:6: The phrase mal'u miqqedem literally reads "they are filled from the east" without naming the imported practices; yaspiqu (Hiphil of sapaq) denotes slapping or clasping hands to seal a bargain or pact, though some relate it to an Aramaic sense "abound with."
native_notes.2:12: The final word weshapel is read here as a Qal consecutive perfect verb ("so that it will be brought low"), matching the verbal usage of shapel in vv. 11 and 17 and the list of lofty objects in vv. 13-16, rather than as an adjective ("and low").
native_notes.2:16: The rare plural construct sekiyyot ("vessels") appears only here in the Hebrew Bible; parallel to "ships of Tarshish," it is widely linked to an Egyptian and Ugaritic term for seagoing craft, though older interpreters derived it from a root meaning "to look at" ("desirable sights" or "works of art").
native_notes.2:20: The Masoretic Text divides lachpor perot into two words, widely understood as a split spelling of the reduplicated animal name chaparparot ("moles" or "shrews," literally "diggers"), paired here with "bats."
native_notes.2:22: The opening Hebrew idiom literally reads "cease for yourselves from man."
native_notes.3:1: The masculine and feminine pairing מַשְׁעֵן וּמַשְׁעֵנָה (lit. "support and prop", both from the root שׁען) is a Hebrew merism expressing every kind of support.
native_notes.3:15: Ketiv reads מלכם (a contracted one-word spelling), while Qere separates it into two words, מַה־לָּכֶם ("what is it to you?"), which is translated here.
native_notes.3:16: Ketiv reads נטוות while Qere reads נְטוּיוֹת (Qal passive participle feminine plural of נטה, "stretched out"); both convey the same sense with an orthographic/morphological variation.
native_notes.3:17: The hapax Piel verb שִׂפַּח is traditionally linked to סַפַּחַת ("scab"), though some take it as "make bare/bald"; פׇּתְהֵן ("their private parts") is a euphemism paired with Piel יְעָרֶה ("expose/lay bare").
native_notes.3:24: The closing phrase כִּי־תַחַת יֹפִי uses the rare noun כִּי ("brand/burn mark", from the root כוה) rather than the conjunction "for", reversing the preceding "instead of X, Y" sequence into a chiastic climax.
native_notes.4:2: The noun צֶמַח literally means "sprout", "shoot", or "growth" (the same noun used of a Davidic figure in Jer 23:5; 33:15; Zech 3:8; 6:12), standing here in parallelism with פְרִי הָאָרֶץ ("the fruit of the land").
native_notes.4:4: The conjunction אִם ("if") with a perfect (רָחַץ) and imperfect (יָדִיחַ) functions temporally ("once/when"); the Piel infinitive בָּעֵר carries the dual sense of "burning" and "purging away".
native_notes.5:1: The idiom בְּקֶרֶן בֶּן־שָׁמֶן literally reads "on a horn, a son of fatness/oil", denoting a fertile hillside or ridge.
native_notes.5:7: The Hebrew employs striking wordplay pairing near-homophones: מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, "justice") with מִשְׂפָּח (mispach, "bloodshed/oppression"), and צְדָקָה (tsedaqah, "righteousness") with צְעָקָה (tse'aqah, "outcry").
native_notes.5:10: A צֶמֶד ("yoke") is the area a pair of oxen could plow in a day (roughly an acre); a בַּת ("bath") is a liquid measure of about 22 liters, and a חֹמֶר ("homer") equals ten אֵיפָה ("ephahs"), indicating a severe crop failure.
native_notes.5:17: The Masoretic text vocalizes מֵחִים ("fat ones", figuratively the wealthy) and גָּרִים (Qal participle of גור, "sojourners/strangers"), whereas the Septuagint reads "lambs".
native_notes.5:29: Ketiv reads ושאג (Qal weqatal, "and it will roar"), while Qere reads יִשְׁאַג (Qal imperfect without the conjunction, "they roar"), which is followed here; throughout 5:26b-30 the Hebrew uses collective singular forms for the invading nations named in 5:26a.
native_notes.6:3: The clause "the fullness of all the earth is His glory" follows the Hebrew construct noun melo ("fullness") literally, meaning that His glory is what fills the entire earth.
native_notes.6:4: Hebrew ammot hassippim ("bases of the thresholds") uses a rare architectural sense of ammah referring to the structural foundations or door-pivots supporting the temple thresholds.
native_notes.6:10: The three Hiphil imperatives literally command making the people's heart "fat" (an idiom for dull and unresponsive), its ears "heavy," and its eyes "smeared shut."
native_notes.6:13: Hebrew lebaer (Piel infinitive construct of b'r) means "for burning" or "for consuming," and beshalleket denotes either the felling of trees or the shedding of leaves, leaving behind a stump (matstsebet).
native_notes.7:1: The singular verbs "went up" and "was not able" agree grammatically with the first-named subject, Rezin; "not able to fight against it" idiomatically expresses inability to capture the city in battle.
native_notes.7:3: The Hebrew name Shear-jashub means "A remnant will return," echoing the verb "turn back" in 6:10.
native_notes.7:9: The concluding warning plays on two stems of the same Hebrew root 'mn: Hiphil ta'aminu ("trust" or "believe") and Niphal te'amenu ("remain firm" or "be established").
native_notes.7:11: The Masoretic pointing she'alah represents the lengthened pausal Qal imperative of sh'l ("ask"), giving "go deep in asking"; an alternative vocalization (she'olah, reflected in several ancient versions) reads "as deep as Sheol."
native_notes.7:14: Hebrew ha'almah denotes a young woman of marriageable age, normally unmarried (rendered parthenos, "virgin," in the Greek Septuagint); Immanuel means "God is with us," and weqara't is an archaic third-person feminine singular form ("and she will call").
native_notes.8:1: Hebrew becheret enosh (literally "with a human stylus") refers to ordinary, legible script; the inscribed name Maher-shalal-hash-baz means "Swift to the plunder, speedy to the prey," prefixed with lamed ("Belonging to").
native_notes.8:6: The Masoretic Hebrew reads umesos ("and rejoicing") with Rezin and the son of Remaliah, an unusual nominal construction continuing the preceding clause; it is translated as written rather than emended to a verb meaning "melt in fear."
native_notes.8:9: Hebrew ro'u is the Qal imperative of r'' ("break" or "shatter"), pairing with wechottu ("and be shattered"); some ancient versions instead reflect a reading from yd' ("know") or r'h ("band together").
native_notes.8:16: Taken here as Isaiah's instruction following the end of the LORD's speech in verse 15 ("my disciples"); some interpreters extend the LORD's speech through verse 16, yielding "My disciples."
native_notes.8:23: In Masoretic versification this verse concludes chapter 8 (numbered 9:1 in another verse division); it contrasts two Hiphil perfects of opposite roots: heqal (from qll, literally "made light" or "dishonored") and hikbid (from kbd, literally "made weighty" or "honored").
native_notes.9:2: Ketiv reads לא ("not"), while Qere, translated here, reads לוֹ ("for it"), referring to the nation.
native_notes.9:4: סְאוֹן סֹאֵן ("boot of one tramping") is a cognate noun and Qal participle occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible, understood via Akkadian and Aramaic cognates as a marching boot or sandal.
native_notes.9:5: וַיִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ uses a Qal active verb with unspecified subject ("and one will call his name" or "and He will call his name"), here rendered with an English passive; the titles פֶּלֶא יוֹעֵץ (lit. "Wonder of a Counselor") and אֲבִי־עַד (lit. "Father of Eternity") pair nouns in apposition or construct.
native_notes.9:6: Ketiv preserves an anomalous final closed mem (ם) in the middle of the word, read by Qere as לְמַרְבֵּה ("of the increase"), derived from the root רבה.
native_notes.9:18: נֶעְתַּם ("has been scorched") is a Niphal perfect of עתם occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible; depending on Semitic cognates it is interpreted either as "scorched" or "darkened."
native_notes.10:4: בִּלְתִּי כָרַע (lit. "except bowing down") is an elliptical construction answering the rhetorical questions of 10:3, meaning nothing remains except to crouch beneath the captives or fall beneath the slaughtered.
native_notes.10:18: כִּמְסֹס נֹסֵס ("like a sick man melting away") combines the Qal infinitive construct of מסס ("melt/waste away") with the Qal participle נֹסֵס, understood from Semitic cognates as a sick or fainting person.
native_notes.10:27: וְחֻבַּל עֹל מִפְּנֵי־שָׁמֶן (lit. "and a yoke will be destroyed because of fatness/oil") is a noted Hebrew crux; following the Masoretic text, it depicts the yoke broken by fatness (or metaphorically by anointing oil).
native_notes.10:29: לָנוּ is vocalized identically to both the Qal perfect 3cp of לוּן ("they spent the night/lodged") and "for us"; taking it as the verb parallels the preceding cognate pair עָבְרוּ מַעְבָּרָה ("they crossed the pass") with מָלוֹן לָנוּ ("they took their night's lodging").
native_notes.10:32: Ketiv reads בית ("house of"), whereas Qere, translated here, reads בַּת ("daughter of"), yielding "Daughter Zion."
native_notes.11:2: The three parallel appositional phrases (ruach chokhmah..., ruach etsah..., ruach da'at...) lack the definite article in Hebrew and may be rendered either capitalized in apposition to "the Spirit of the LORD" or lowercase ("a spirit of wisdom...").
native_notes.11:3: וַהֲרִיחוֹ ("and his delight") is a Hiphil infinitive construct of רוח ("smell") with a 3ms suffix, literally "his smelling," an idiom for taking pleasure or delight in the fear of the LORD.
native_notes.11:8: Both the noun מְאוּרַת ("den") and the Qal perfect verb הָדָה ("stretch out") occur only here in the Hebrew Bible, with their senses inferred from context and parallelism.
native_notes.11:13: צֹרְרֵי יְהוּדָה (Qal participle construct of צרר + "Judah") can be read objectively as "the adversaries of Judah" or subjectively as "the hostile ones of Judah," paralleling the final clause of the verse.
native_notes.11:15: The Masoretic text reads וְהֶחֱרִים (Hiphil of חרם, "completely destroy") rather than "dry up" (חרב) reflected in some ancient versions. בַּעְיָם ("with the scorching heat") is a unique form whose exact etymology is uncertain, traditionally understood as glowing heat or fierce strength.
native_notes.12:1: The verb yashov ("has turned back") is a short prefix form (jussive/preterite) of shuv paired with the Piel imperfect utenachameni ("and You comfort me"), expressing either fulfilled deliverance or a petition ("may Your anger turn back").
native_notes.12:2: The Hebrew pairs the shortened poetic form of the divine name directly with the full divine name, rendered here as "the LORD, the LORD," echoing Exodus 15:2.
native_notes.12:5: Ketiv/Qere: The Qere reads the Hophal feminine participle muda'at ("made known"), while the unvocalized Ketiv spells the word with a yod (myd't, likely a Pual participle with the same passive sense).
native_notes.13:6: The Hebrew creates a wordplay between shod ("devastation") and Shaddai ("the Almighty").
native_notes.13:16: Ketiv/Qere: The Qere substitutes the euphemistic Niphal form tishshakhavnah ("be lain with," rendered "be violated") for the blunter Ketiv verb shagal ("be ravished").
native_notes.13:21: Several desert fauna terms in 13:21-22 (tsiyyim, ochim, benot ya'anah, se'irim, iyyim, tannim) are partly uncertain; se'irim literally means "hairy ones" and can denote either wild goats or goat-like demons.
native_notes.13:22: The MT spells "its citadels" as almenotav (with lamed rather than the usual resh in armenotav), either a phonetic variant or a wordplay on almanah ("widow"), suggesting widowed palaces.
native_notes.14:4: The MT reads the hapax legomenon madhevah, traditionally derived from Aramaic dehav ("gold") and rendered "exaction of gold"; the Dead Sea Scroll 1QIsa-a and ancient versions point instead to marhevah ("insolent fury").
native_notes.14:9: Hebrew repha'im denotes the shades or departed spirits in Sheol, and attudey arets ("leaders of the earth") literally means "he-goats of the earth," a metaphor for rulers.
native_notes.14:12: Hebrew heylel ("Shining One," from halal, "to shine") designates the bright morning star (Venus); the Latin Vulgate rendered it as Lucifer ("light-bearer").
native_notes.14:19: The phrase levush harugim meto'aney charev literally depicts the king as "clothed with those killed, pierced by the sword," using the hapax Pual participle meto'aney ("pierced").
native_notes.14:30: "Firstborn of the poor" (bekhorey dallim) is a Hebrew superlative idiom for the poorest of the poor; in the final clause, the MT shifts from first-person singular ("I will put ... to death") to third-person singular yaharog ("he will kill"), referring to the coming northern invader.
native_notes.15:2: Hebrew habbayit literally means "the house" and is taken here as a Moabite town name (Bayith) paired with Dibon following the Masoretic disjunctive accent on Dibon; alternatively, "he [Moab] has gone up to the temple, and Dibon to the high places."
native_notes.15:3: The phrase "going down in weeping" renders the Hebrew Qal participle yored babbeki, a vivid idiom for collapsing or dissolving in tears.
native_notes.15:5: Hebrew beriheha is a defective plural of bariah ("fugitives"; or from beriah, "bars"). "Eglath-shelishiyah" is taken as a Moabite place name near Zoar (literally "third Eglath" or "a three-year-old heifer"); the rare verb ye'o'eru ("they stir up") is a reduplicated stem form of 'ur ("rouse").
native_notes.15:7: Hebrew yitrah 'asah is an asyndetic relative clause with a singular verb for collective Moab ("the surplus it has acquired"), shifting immediately to plural suffixes and verb ("their stored possessions they carry"). "Wadi of the Willows" (nahal ha'aravim) may also refer to Euphrates poplars or to the Arabah.
native_notes.16:3: Ketiv reads Hiphil masculine plural imperative havi'u ("Bring," pl.); Qere reads feminine singular havi'i ("Bring," fem. sg.), matching the following feminine singular imperatives and suffixes.
native_notes.16:4: The Masoretic Text points niddahay ("My outcasts," Niphal participle with first-person suffix) followed by a disjunctive accent before vocative "Moab"; some ancient versions read construct niddahei mo'av ("the outcasts of Moab").
native_notes.16:7: Hebrew 'ashishei ("raisin cakes") fits the vineyard imagery of vv. 8-10; some older interpreters render it "foundations" from a different root, and the parallel in Jer 48:31 reads "men."
native_notes.16:8: In "the lords of the nations have struck down its choice vines," standard Hebrew word order treats "the lords of the nations" as subject of halemu (Qal of halam); alternatively, "its choice vines" is subject ("struck down [intoxicated] the lords of the nations").
native_notes.16:9: Hebrew 'arayyawek ("I will soak you") is an anomalous Piel imperfect of rawah with a second-person feminine singular suffix. Hebrew hedad ("the shouting") in vv. 9-10 carries a deliberate double sense, evoking both enemy battle cries falling on the harvest and joyous vintage shouts now silenced.
native_notes.17:6: Hebrew bis'ifeha poriyyah ("on the branches of a fruit-bearing tree") uses an anticipatory feminine singular suffix ("its branches") explained by the appositional Qal feminine active participle poriyyah ("fruit-bearing").
native_notes.17:9: The Masoretic Text reads hahoresh weha'amir ("the woodland and the summit/topmost bough," echoing 'amir in v. 6); the Septuagint reflects a different consonantal reading ("the Hivites and the Amorites").
native_notes.17:11: Hebrew tesagsegi ("you make it grow") is a hapax legomenon (Pilpel imperfect), alternatively derived from sug ("hedge/fence in"). Hebrew ned ("gone") is taken as a verbal form from nud ("flee/vanish"), though as pointed it also resembles the noun ned ("a heap"); nahalah ("sickness," from halah) puns on nahalah ("inheritance").
native_notes.17:13: Hebrew shifts to collective masculine singular forms in vv. 13-14 (bo, "it/him"; nas, "flees"; ruddaf, Pual "is pursued"; 'einennu, "it is no more") referring to the assembled nations; these are smoothed to plural "them/they" in English.
native_notes.18:1: "Buzzing wings" translates a rare construct phrase (tsiltsal kenafayim) from an onomatopoeic root meaning "buzz" or "whir" (cf. Deut 28:42), though some connect it to a homonymous root meaning "shadow."
native_notes.18:2: Several rare expressions appear here: "tall and smooth" is literally "drawn out and burnished" (Pual participles of mashakh and marat); "far and wide" is literally "from it and onward"; "might and trampling" renders an obscure reduplicated form (qav-qav) paired with "trampling"; and "cut through" translates a rare verb (baza) attested only here and in 18:7.
native_notes.18:4: The ketiv spells the verb plene (with a vav) while the qere spells it defectively (without a vav); both represent the Qal 1st-person singular cohortative of shaqat ("stay quiet"). The Masoretic Text also reads "in the heat of harvest."
native_notes.18:7: The Masoretic Text has the preposition "from" (min) only before the second phrase ("and from a people"), either serving poetic double duty for the first phrase as well or leaving "a people tall and smooth" in apposition to "tribute."
native_notes.19:6: "Will grow foul" renders an unusual double-prefixed Hiphil form (he'eznichu) of zanach ("stink/grow foul"). "Egypt" in "channels of Egypt" translates Matsor, a singular poetic form of the Hebrew name Mitsrayim.
native_notes.19:10: "Its pillars" translates shatoteha (literally "its foundations/pillars," cf. Ps 11:3, used figuratively of leading citizens), though some derive it from a weaving term ("its weavers"). "All who work for wages" translates the Masoretic Text (osey seker) literally.
native_notes.19:12: The Masoretic Text reads a Qal jussive (veyed'u, "and let them know"), rather than a causative Hiphil ("make known").
native_notes.19:18: The Masoretic Text reads Ir ha-Heres ("City of Destruction"); the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) and some Hebrew manuscripts read Ir ha-Cheres ("City of the Sun," i.e., Heliopolis).
native_notes.19:23: The particle et before "Assyria" is taken here as the preposition "with," continuing the cultic sense of "worship" (avad) from 19:21, though grammatically et could also mark a direct object ("serve Assyria").
native_notes.20:1: "The chief commander" translates Hebrew tartan, a loanword from the Assyrian military title turtanu ("commander-in-chief").
native_notes.20:2: "Your sandals from your feet" translates collective singular forms in the Masoretic Text (literally "your sandal from your foot").
native_notes.20:4: "With bared buttocks" translates a rare Qal passive participle masculine plural construct (chasufay) with the noun shet ("buttocks," cf. 2 Sam 10:4).
native_notes.21:2: Hebrew אַנְחָתָה lacks a mappiq in the final ה, traditionally understood as "her groaning" (an unpointed 3fs suffix referring to the groaning caused by Babylon) or simply "groaning."
native_notes.21:5: The phrase צָפֹה הַצָּפִית pairs a Qal infinitive absolute with the hapax legomenon צָפִית, meaning either "spread the rugs" (from צפה II, "spread out") or "keep the watch" (from צפה I, "watch").
native_notes.21:8: The Masoretic Text reads וַיִּקְרָא אַרְיֵה, literally "and he cried out, a lion" (taken comparatively as "like a lion"); this translation follows the MT rather than emending אַרְיֵה to הָרֹאֶה ("the seer/lookout").
native_notes.21:12: The verbs אָתָה / אֵתָיוּ ("come") and תִּבְעָיוּן / בְּעָיוּ ("inquire") employ Aramaizing roots and forms fitting this pronouncement concerning Seir and Dumah.
native_notes.22:5: The phrase מְקַרְקַר קִר combines the Pilpel participle of קרר/קור ("tearing down") with the defective spelling קִר ("wall"), creating wordplay that also anticipates the proper name Kir (קִיר) in v. 6.
native_notes.22:16: The participles חֹצְבִי ("hewing out") and חֹקְקִי ("chiseling") carry the poetic binding vowel (hireq compaginis) rather than a first-person suffix, while the verse shifts abruptly to third-person suffixes ("his tomb," "for himself").
native_notes.22:17: The Qal participle and infinitive absolute עֹטְךָ עָטֹה (from עטה) mean "wrap you up completely" (preparing for the ball-winding image of v. 18), though some lexicons render the root here as "grasp firmly."
native_notes.22:19: The Masoretic Text shifts within the verse from first person (וַהֲדַפְתִּיךָ, "I will push you out") to third person (יֶהֶרְסֶךָ, "He will pull you down"), both referring to the LORD.
native_notes.22:24: Hebrew כְּבוֹד ("glory") also carries its root sense of "weight," linking the "throne of glory" (v. 23) with the "load" hanging on the peg (v. 25).
native_notes.23:1: Hebrew מִבַּיִת מִבּוֹא uses privative מִן twice, literally "from a house, from entering," indicating Tyre is devastated so that neither house nor entry/harbor remains.
native_notes.23:10: The Masoretic Text reads עִבְרִי ("overflow/pass over," Qal imperative of עבר) rather than the Septuagint's "till"; the rare noun מֵזַח denotes a "belt" or "girdle" (cf. Ps 109:19), used figuratively here for "restraint."
native_notes.23:12: Ketiv reads כתיים and Qere reads כִּתִּים, an orthographic variant for the same place name, "Kittim" (Cyprus).
native_notes.23:13: Qere reads בַחוּנָיו ("its/their siege towers," with 3ms suffix referring to Assyria) where Ketiv reads בחיניו; the clause זֶה הָעָם לֹא הָיָה is literally "this is the people that was not," expressing that it is no more.
native_notes.24:6: Hebrew charu is the Qal perfect of charar ("be scorched, burned"), matching the consuming curse earlier in the verse.
native_notes.24:15: Hebrew ba'urim literally means "in the lights" or "in the fires," widely understood as the regions of sunrise in the east, balancing "the coastlands of the sea" in the west.
native_notes.24:16: Hebrew razi-li literally means "wasting away to me" (from razah, "grow lean, waste away"), paralleling "Woe to me!" rather than referring to a secret.
native_notes.25:5: Hebrew ya'aneh is the Qal imperfect of anah ("be bowed down, humbled"), conveying that the song of the ruthless is brought low just as scorching heat is subdued by a cloud's shade.
native_notes.25:10: Following the qere bemo (poetic form of the preposition "in") for "in a dung pit"; the ketiv reads bemei ("in the waters of").
native_notes.25:11: Hebrew orbot yadav ("craftiness of his hands") uses a hapax legomenon from the root arab ("lie in wait, scheme"), denoting the artifice or cunning skill of Moab's hands.
native_notes.26:4: The Hebrew pairs the shortened poetic form of the divine name with the full divine name and uses a beth essentiae ("the LORD, the LORD, is an eternal Rock").
native_notes.26:16: Hebrew tsaqun is a rare Qal perfect third-person plural of tsuq ("pour out") with a paragogic nun.
native_notes.26:18: Hebrew yipplu (Qal imperfect of naphal) literally means "fall"; some understand it in the sense of "be born," continuing the childbirth imagery of vv. 17-18 and anticipating the Hiphil tappil ("bring forth") in v. 19.
native_notes.26:19: Masoretic nevelati literally reads "my corpse," used collectively with the plural verb yequmun ("will rise") to express the speaker's solidarity with God's dead; Hebrew orot ("lights") is also taken by some as "herbs."
native_notes.26:20: Following the qere delatekha (singular, "your door"); the ketiv reads delateikha (plural, "your doors").
native_notes.27:2: Masoretic Hebrew reads chemer ("wine"), yielding "a vineyard of wine" (some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint read chemed, "delight/pleasantness"). The verb is a Piel imperative of anah ("sing").
native_notes.27:4: The phrase mi-yitteneni (literally "who will give me") is a Hebrew wish idiom ("if only"). The feminine singular suffixes translated "them" refer collectively to the briers and thorns.
native_notes.27:7: Masoretic Hebrew has the Qal passive participle harugav ("those killed by Him," or "his killed ones") rather than an active participle ("his killers"), pairing three forms of nkh ("strike") with three forms of hrg ("kill/slaughter").
native_notes.27:8: The rare form bese'se'ah is commonly analyzed as a reduplication of se'ah (a dry measure), hence "measure by measure," though some understand it as "by driving away." The Qal perfect hagah here means "removed" or "drove away."
native_notes.27:12: "The River" refers to the Euphrates, and shibbolet ("channel/flowing stream") plays on its homonym meaning "ear of grain," echoing the harvest verb chavat ("beat out grain/thresh").
native_notes.28:10: The Hebrew tsav la-tsav, tsav la-tsav, qav la-qav, qav la-qav uses staccato monosyllabic wordplay ("command after command ... line after line") that mocks the prophet's teaching while mimicking childish or drunken repetition.
native_notes.28:15: Two ketiv/qere variants follow the qere: qere shot ("scourge," matching v. 18) for ketiv shayit, and qere Qal imperfect ya'avor ("passes through") for ketiv Qal perfect avar.
native_notes.28:16: Masoretic Hebrew points the verb as a Piel perfect yissad ("has laid") after hineni ("look, I"). The final clause lo yachish literally means "will not hasten," that is, will not act or flee in panic.
native_notes.28:28: Opening with an unmarked rhetorical question, the verse repeats the root dqq ("crush": Hophal imperfect yudaq and Qal imperfect yeduqqennu) and uses the unusual infinitive absolute spelling adosh (for dosh) to express continuous threshing.
native_notes.29:2: "Ariel" plays on its dual resonance as "lion of God" and "altar hearth" (compare Ezek 43:15-16), following the assonant pair ta'aniyyah wa-'aniyyah ("moaning and mourning").
native_notes.29:6: The Niphal imperfect tippaqed is 3rd feminine singular ("she will be visited"), referring to Ariel and shifting from the 2nd feminine singular address of vv. 3-5 to the 3rd feminine singular pronouns of v. 7.
native_notes.29:9: The Hithpalpel imperative hitmahmehu ("delay/linger," from mhh) plays on the sound of the Qal imperative temahu ("be astounded," from tmh), and the second half shifts to Qal perfects ("they are drunk ... they stagger").
native_notes.29:11: Ketiv reads hassefer ("the scroll/writing") with the definite article; the qere omits the article (sefer, matching v. 12) in the idiom yodea sefer (literally "one who knows writing," that is, "knows how to read").
native_notes.29:13: Masoretic Hebrew points richaq as a Piel perfect ("they have kept far"), and the Pual participle melummadah ("taught/learned") modifies "commandment of men."
native_notes.30:1: "Seal an alliance" translates Hebrew linsok massekah (Qal infinitive construct of nsk plus cognate noun), literally "to pour out a libation" or "to weave a covering," an idiom for ratifying a treaty.
native_notes.30:7: The difficult Hebrew clause rahab hem shabet is literally "Rahab, they [are] sitting/inaction," using the Qal infinitive construct shabet (from yshb "sit" or shbt "cease") as an ironic nickname mocking Egypt's boastful power.
native_notes.30:8: Masoretic vocalization reads la'ad ("forever"), whereas the unvocalized consonants can be read le'ed ("as a witness") as in several ancient versions; translated strictly according to the Masoretic Text.
native_notes.30:20: Hebrew morekha is morphologically plural ("your teachers"), yet its verb yikkanef (Niphal imperfect 3ms of knf, hapax legomenon, "hide oneself") is singular, indicating an honorific singular ("your Teacher").
native_notes.30:32: Translated per the Qere bam ("against them") rather than the Ketiv bh ("against her"). Hebrew matteh musadah literally means "staff of appointment" or "staff of foundation."
native_notes.30:33: Translated per the Qere hi (feminine singular, matching the feminine suffixes later in the verse) rather than the Ketiv hu (masculine singular); both refer to Topheth ("it").
native_notes.31:5: Hebrew pairs two Qal infinitives absolute with Hiphil verbs (ganon wehitsil pasoah wehimlit), using pasoah—the Passover verb—for "passing over" or "sparing."
native_notes.31:6: The 2mp imperative shubu ("Return") shifts to the 3mp Hiphil perfect he'miqu ("have deeply revolted"), taking "the sons of Israel" as its subject (alternatively a vocative, "from whom they have deeply revolted, sons of Israel").
native_notes.31:9: "His rock" (sal'o) metaphorically denotes Assyria's ruler or stronghold, and "at the standard" (minnes) plays on "will flee" (wenas) in v. 8.
native_notes.32:7: Translated per the Qere aniyyim ("the poor/afflicted") rather than the Ketiv anawim ("the humble"). Hebrew also plays on kelay ("scoundrel") and kelaw ("his devices").
native_notes.32:11: The four imperatives regazah, peshotah, orah, and hagorah take an unusual -ah form for feminine plural addressees, and "wrap your waists" (hagor al-halatsayim) elliptically omits sackcloth.
native_notes.32:15: Hebrew ruach ("spirit") lacks the definite article here and may be read either as "a spirit" (or "wind") or as "the Spirit" poured out from on high. "And the orchard" follows the Qere wehakkarmel (with the definite article) rather than the Ketiv wekarmel ("and an orchard").
native_notes.32:19: The hapax verb ubarad ("it will hail") plays on the sound of beredet ("when ... comes down"), followed by the cognate emphasis ubashshiflah tishpal ("in lowliness ... will be brought low").
native_notes.33:1: The phrase 'when you cease' translates the rare MT form kanneloteka, traditionally derived from a hapax root nlh parallel in sense to tmm ('finish') in the preceding clause.
native_notes.33:2: The MT reads 'their arm' with a third-person plural suffix, shifting briefly from the first-person plural petitions ('us,' 'our') surrounding it.
native_notes.33:7: The hapax legomenon 'er'ellam ('their valiant ones') is traditionally linked to 'ari'el ('hero, lion-like warrior'; cf. 2 Sam 23:20) with a third-person plural suffix.
native_notes.33:23: The MT shifts abruptly to feminine singular ('your cords') and plural ('their mast') nautical imagery; 'booty' renders the rare noun 'ad (cf. Gen 49:27; Zeph 3:8) paired with shalal ('spoil').
native_notes.34:6: The verb 'made rich with fat' renders the rare Hothpaal passive-reflexive stem of dshn (huddashnah), echoed by the Pual form of the same root in v. 7.
native_notes.34:11: The exact species denoted by several desert animals in vv. 11 and 14-15 are uncertain; 'measuring line of formlessness and the plumb stones of emptiness' echoes tohu wabohu in Gen 1:2.
native_notes.34:12: The MT syntax in the first clause is highly compressed, literally reading 'its nobles--and there is none there--a kingdom they will proclaim,' meaning no noble remains there to proclaim kingship.
native_notes.34:14: The hapax noun lilit ('night creature,' often transliterated 'Lilith') refers to a nocturnal bird or night demon in ancient Near Eastern lore.
native_notes.34:16: The MT shifts directly from first person ('My mouth,' pi) to third person ('His Spirit,' rucho), with emphatic independent pronouns reinforcing each subject.
native_notes.35:1: The MT verb yesusum ('will be glad') displays an unusual final -m ending on a third-person plural Qal imperfect of sws, often explained as assimilation of a paragogic nun before the initial m of midbar ('wilderness').
native_notes.35:7: The noun sharab can mean either 'mirage' or 'scorching heat/ground' (cf. Isa 49:10); in the second half, chatsir ('grass') may also be taken as its homonym meaning 'abode/enclosure' (echoing 34:13).
native_notes.35:8: The clause wehu'-lamo ('but it will be for them') is syntactically terse; taking lamo as plural ('for them,' following the Masoretic punctuation) distinguishes the redeemed travelers from the unclean, though some construe lamo as singular ('for him who walks the way').
native_notes.36:2: Rabshakeh is an Assyrian official title (Akkadian rab-shaqe, chief cupbearer or high officer) treated here without the Hebrew definite article.
native_notes.36:5: Masoretic Isaiah reads the first-person Qal perfect "I say" (amarti), whereas the parallel in 2 Kings 18:20 reads the second-person "you say" (amarta).
native_notes.36:12: Ketiv/Qere: the Masoretic qere substitutes the euphemisms "their excrement" (tso'atam) and "the water of their feet" (meme raglehem) for the blunter written ketiv forms meaning "their dung" and "their urine."
native_notes.36:16: "Make peace with me" literally reads "make a blessing (berakhah) with me," an idiom for concluding a peaceful settlement or treaty of submission.
native_notes.37:18: Masoretic Isaiah literally reads "all the lands/countries (ha'aratsot) and their land (artsam)," whereas the parallel in 2 Kings 19:17 reads "the nations (haggoyim) and their land."
native_notes.37:21: Masoretic Isaiah omits the verb "I have heard" found at the end of 2 Kings 19:20, linking the causal clause ("Because you have prayed to Me...") directly into v. 22.
native_notes.37:24: "Its farthest height" translates Masoretic Isaiah's merom qitso, whereas the parallel in 2 Kings 19:23 reads "its farthest lodging place" (melon qitso).
native_notes.37:27: "Of little strength" renders the idiom qitsre-yad (lit. "short of hand"). At the end of the verse, Masoretic Isaiah reads "a field (shedemah) before the standing grain," whereas 2 Kings 19:26 reads "blighted grain" (shedephah).
native_notes.37:30: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv reads a Qal infinitive absolute ("and eating"), while the read qere conforms to the preceding imperatives with the second-person masculine plural Qal imperative "and eat" (we'ikhlu).
native_notes.38:8: Hebrew ma'alot literally means "steps" or "stairway," possibly a stepped structure serving as a sundial; the feminine verb yaredah ("has gone down") agrees grammatically with feminine shemesh ("sun").
native_notes.38:10: Hebrew bidmi is rare and may mean either "at the midpoint" or "in the stillness/cutting off" of his days; puqqadti (Pual of paqad) means "I have been deprived of."
native_notes.38:11: Hebrew doubles the shortened divine name Yah ("the LORD, the LORD"). At the end of the verse, the Masoretic Text reads chadel ("cessation" or "transience," understood here as the transient world), often compared to cheled ("world").
native_notes.38:16: The Hebrew is terse: "by these things" (alehem) refers back to God's word and deeds in v. 15, and the Hiphil verb tachalimeni (from chalam II) means "restore to health."
native_notes.38:17: The Masoretic Text reads chashaqta (Qal of chashaq, "loved/clung to"), used in a pregnant construction with min to mean "lovingly kept back from."
native_notes.39:1: The verb vayyechezaq ("and had grown strong again," Qal of chazaq) creates a Hebrew wordplay on the name Hezekiah (Chizqiyyahu).
native_notes.39:2: Hebrew bet nekotoh ("his treasure house") uses an archaic third-person masculine singular suffix and a loanword related to Akkadian bit nakamti ("storehouse").
native_notes.39:7: Hebrew yiqqachu is a pausal Qal imperfect third-person masculine plural of laqach with an indefinite subject ("they will take"), rendered passively here as "will be taken."
native_notes.40:3: Both the Masoretic accentuation (zaqeph qaton on qore) and the poetic parallelism ("in the wilderness" // "in the desert plain") link "in the wilderness" with "clear the way" rather than with "a voice calls out."
native_notes.40:6: The Masoretic Text reads third-person va'amar ("and he said") rather than first-person ("and I said") found in some ancient witnesses; chasdo ("its loyal love," from chesed) describes how short-lived human constancy is (cf. Hos 6:4), though it may also suggest loveliness.
native_notes.40:9: The construct phrase mebasseret tsiyyon (and parallel mebasseret yerushalayim) can be read either appositionally ("Zion, messenger of good news," matching the feminine singular imperatives addressed to the city) or objectively ("messenger of good news to Zion").
native_notes.40:20: The Masoretic Text points hamesukkan as a Pual participle ("the one too poor for an offering," cf. misken in Eccl 4:13); some lexicographers connect the consonants to Akkadian musukkannu, a durable hardwood.
native_notes.40:21: The Masoretic Text has no preposition "from" before mosdot ha'arets, allowing it to be read directly as the object of "understood" ("understood the foundations of the earth"), though some carry over "from" from the previous clause.
native_notes.41:2: The Hebrew clause "righteousness calls/meets him at his foot" is syntactically ambiguous: it may take tsedeq adverbially with God as subject ("whom He calls in righteousness to follow Him," cf. 42:6; 45:13) or as subject ("whom righteousness meets at every step"). The verb yard is an apocopated form of radah ("subdue, have dominion over").
native_notes.41:10: The verb tishta is the Hithpael jussive of sha'ah ("look about in alarm" or "gaze around anxiously"; the same stem recurs in 41:23). "The right hand of My righteousness" preserves the literal Hebrew construct chain.
native_notes.41:23: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere reads wenir'eh (Qal imperfect 1cp of ra'ah, "and we will see/look"), which is followed here; the Ketiv lacks the final he and could be read either as a shortened spelling of ra'ah or as defective wenira from yare ("and we will fear").
native_notes.41:24: The noun epha ("nothingness") is a hapax legomenon parallel to ayin ("nothing"), generally understood as a poetic variant of ephes ("nothingness").
native_notes.41:27: The opening clause in the Masoretic Text is elliptically compressed (literally, "First to Zion: 'Look, here they are!'"), leaving the verb of speaking implied.
native_notes.42:4: The verbs yikheh (Qal imperfect of kahah, "grow dim") and yaruts (Qal imperfect of ratsats formed on the analogy of hollow verbs, "be crushed") deliberately echo the adjective kehah ("dim") and Qal passive participle ratsuts ("crushed") in 42:3.
native_notes.42:19: Meshullam is the Pual participle of shalem ("be complete, at peace"), variously understood as "one at peace," "covenant partner," or "dedicated one." The Masoretic Text repeats iwwer ("blind") in both halves of the second question.
native_notes.42:20: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere reads ra'ot (a Qal infinitive absolute form of ra'ah, "seeing," paralleling the Qal infinitive absolute paqoah, "opening"), whereas the Ketiv represents the Qal perfect 2ms ra'ita ("you have seen"). The Masoretic Text also shifts from second-person "you observe" to third-person "he hears."
native_notes.42:22: Hapeah is a Hiphil infinitive absolute of puah (denominative from pah, "snare"), functioning here with passive force ("ensnared"), and bahurim is vocalized as the preposition be with the article plus hurim ("in holes"), paralleling "in prison houses."
native_notes.42:24: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere reads limshissah ("as spoil/plunder," matching meshissah in 42:22), whereas the Ketiv could be read either as an orthographic variant of the same noun or as a Poel participle ("to the despoiler"). The Masoretic Text shifts from first-person plural "we have sinned" to third-person plural "they were unwilling... they did not listen."
native_notes.43:8: The opening verb has the Masoretic pointing of a Hiphil perfect or infinitive construct rather than the standard imperative form, but in this courtroom summons it functions as an imperative ('Bring out').
native_notes.43:9: The verb 'gather together' has the form of a Niphal perfect ('have gathered'), functioning here as a summons parallel to the following Niphal jussive ('let the peoples assemble').
native_notes.43:13: 'From the first day' renders a terse Hebrew phrase literally meaning 'from day,' idiomatically denoting 'from the beginning of time' or 'from eternity.'
native_notes.43:14: The Masoretic pointing reads 'fugitives' (whereas a different vowel pattern of the same consonants means 'bars'); the closing phrase literally reads 'in the ships of their shouting' or 'jubilation.'
native_notes.44:9: In the Masoretic Text, the pronoun rendered 'themselves' carries ancient scribal dots (puncta extraordinaria) marking an early textual query, while remaining in the text.
native_notes.44:12: The opening clause is syntactically elliptical in Hebrew (literally 'craftsman of iron, a cutting tool, and he works over the coals'), with the tool serving as the object or instrument of the following verb.
native_notes.44:18: 'Have been plastered shut' translates a third-person masculine singular Qal active verb (literally 'he has plastered over'), functioning either as an impersonal passive or with God as the implied subject.
native_notes.44:21: 'You will not be forgotten by Me' renders a rare Niphal imperfect carrying a first-person pronominal suffix (literally 'you will not be forgotten to/by Me'), though some construe it actively as 'do not forget Me.'
native_notes.44:24: Translated following the Qere ('by Myself,' literally 'from with Me'); the Ketiv divides the consonants into two words meaning 'who was with Me?'
native_notes.45:2: Qere אֲיַשֵּׁר (Piel, "I will make level") is translated; Ketiv אושר represents the Hiphil of the same root ישר with the same sense. The rare plural הֲדוּרִים ("rugged terrain") literally denotes swollen or uneven ground.
native_notes.45:7: Hebrew רָע ("disaster"), paired directly with שָׁלוֹם ("peace"), denotes calamity or adversity rather than moral evil.
native_notes.45:9: The clause וּפׇעׇלְךָ אֵין־יָדַיִם לוֹ is syntactically compressed and may be read either as part of the clay's speech ("Your work has no hands/handles") or as an elliptical question ("or will your work say, 'He has no hands'?").
native_notes.45:11: Following the Masoretic vocalization and accents, שְׁאָלוּנִי ("Ask Me") is a Qal imperative, while the Piel imperfect תְּצַוֻּנִי ("will you command Me?") functions as an unmarked rhetorical question governing both prepositional phrases that precede it.
native_notes.45:19: Hebrew תֹּהוּ ("in vain," literally "emptiness") echoes תֹהוּ ("wasteland") in 45:18, linking God's purposeful creation of the earth with His clear self-revelation to Israel.
native_notes.46:8: The Hithpolel imperative הִתְאֹשָׁשׁוּ ("be resolute") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; its sense is generally connected with standing firm or taking courage.
native_notes.46:11: Qere עֲצָתִי ("My counsel") is translated, matching עֲצָתִי in 46:10; Ketiv עצתו reads "his counsel."
native_notes.46:12: Hebrew אַבִּירֵי לֵב literally means "strong of heart," used here idiomatically for obstinacy ("stubborn of heart").
native_notes.47:3: Hebrew וְלֹא אֶפְגַּע אָדָם literally means "and I will not meet a human," a difficult idiom understood here as "I will spare no human" (or alternatively "I will not accept any human intercession").
native_notes.47:9: The preposition בְּ before both "your many sorceries" and "the exceeding power of your spells" carries a concessive force ("in spite of"), anticipating the ironic challenge in 47:12.
native_notes.47:11: Hebrew שַׁחְרָהּ is taken as a Piel infinitive construct ("charm it away"), matching the parallel Piel infinitive כַּפְּרָהּ ("buy it off"); alternatively, it may be derived from the noun שַׁחַר ("its dawn"). Hebrew רָעָה ("disaster") also plays on רָעָתֵךְ ("your wickedness") in 47:10.
native_notes.47:13: Qere הֹבְרֵי ("those who divide," Qal active participle construct of the hapax root הבר, referring to astrologers partitioning the sky) is translated; Ketiv הברו reads a plural perfect verb ("they divided") or an archaic spelling.
native_notes.48:1: The Hebrew literally reads "from the waters of Judah," using "waters" as a poetic idiom for physical descent or lineage.
native_notes.48:10: The Hebrew Qal verb normally means "I have chosen you," though in parallel with "refined" and "smelting furnace" it is widely understood as a cognate or byform meaning "test, examine."
native_notes.48:11: The Niphal imperfect verb "could be profaned" has no expressed subject in the Masoretic Text; it refers back to "My name" in verse 9.
native_notes.48:16: The final clause shifts from the LORD's direct speech to the messenger or Servant; the syntax of "and His Spirit" allows it to be read either as a second subject alongside the Lord GOD or as a second object sent with the speaker.
native_notes.48:19: The Hebrew forms a wordplay between "your body" and the rare noun rendered "its grains," referring to the grains of sand.
native_notes.49:5: Following the Qere (read form) "to Him"; the Ketiv (written form) reads "not," which would yield "though Israel is not gathered."
native_notes.49:6: Following the Qere (read form), a Qal passive participle meaning "the preserved ones of"; the Ketiv (written form) is a related adjectival spelling with the same sense.
native_notes.49:13: Following the Qere (read form), a Qal imperative with the conjunction ("and burst forth"); the Ketiv (written form) lacks the conjunction and is an imperfect ("they will burst forth").
native_notes.49:17: The Masoretic Text vocalizes the noun as "your sons"; an alternative ancient tradition vocalizes the same consonants as "your builders."
native_notes.49:24: The Masoretic Text reads "a righteous one" (sometimes understood as a rightful captor), in contrast to "a tyrant" in verse 25.
native_notes.50:4: The Hebrew infinitive rendered "to sustain" occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and is understood from comparative Semitic evidence and context to mean "to support, help, sustain."
native_notes.50:8: Literally "the master of my legal case," a Hebrew forensic idiom for an adversary or opponent in a lawsuit.
native_notes.50:11: The Piel participle literally means "girding yourselves with" or "equipping yourselves with" firebrands, picturing hostile adversaries arming themselves with flaming weapons.
native_notes.51:4: Hebrew אַרְגִּיעַ (Hiphil imperfect 1cs of רגע II, 'settle, establish, give rest') is used transitively with מִשְׁפָּטִי ('My justice') to express establishing justice firmly as a light to the peoples.
native_notes.51:6: Hebrew כְּמוֹ־כֵן literally means 'like so, in the same way,' though some lexicons take כֵן as a singular related to כִּנִּים ('gnats'), rendering 'like gnats.' Hebrew נִמְלָחוּ is a Niphal perfect 3cp of מלח II ('dissipate, disperse, be torn to shreds').
native_notes.51:14: Hebrew צֹעֶה (Qal active participle ms of צעה, 'stoop, bend over') depicts a captive bowed down in chains, while לְהִפָּתֵחַ (Niphal infinitive construct of פתח) means 'to be loosed' or 'released.'
native_notes.51:16: The Masoretic Text reads לִנְטֹעַ (Qal infinitive construct of נטע, 'to plant,' used of pitching tents in Dan 11:45), rather than לִנְטוֹת ('to stretch out') as in v. 13.
native_notes.51:19: The Masoretic Text has the 1cs Piel imperfect אֲנַחֲמֵךְ ('I comfort you') with interrogative מִי used idiomatically in the sense 'how?' (compare Amos 7:2, 5), rather than a 3ms verb ('who will comfort you?').
native_notes.52:2: Ketiv reads התפתחו (3cp Hithpael perfect 'they have loosed themselves' or 2mp imperative); the Qere הִתְפַּתְּחִי (2fs Hithpael imperative of פתח, 'loose from yourself') is translated here to match the surrounding feminine singular imperatives addressed to Jerusalem.
native_notes.52:5: Hebrew יְהֵילִילוּ (Hiphil imperfect 3mp of ילל, unusually retaining the Hiphil ה) normally means 'howl' or 'wail,' here expressing the rulers' mocking or boastful cries. Hebrew מִנֹּאָץ is a Hithpoel participle of נאץ with assimilated ת, meaning 'continually treated with contempt.'
native_notes.52:13: Hebrew יַשְׂכִּיל (Hiphil imperfect 3ms of שׂכל) combines the senses of acting with wisdom or insight and achieving success or prosperity.
native_notes.52:14: The Masoretic Text shifts abruptly from 2ms עָלֶיךָ ('at you') to 3ms מַרְאֵהוּ ('his appearance') and וְתֹאֲרוֹ ('and his form'). Hebrew מִשְׁחַת is a rare construct noun from שׁחת ('disfigurement, marring'), introducing an explanatory aside before the correlative כֵּן ('so') resumes in v. 15.
native_notes.52:15: Hebrew יַזֶּה (Hiphil imperfect 3ms of נזה) elsewhere consistently means 'sprinkle' (typically in ritual purification), though some scholars derive it from a homonymous root meaning 'startle.'
native_notes.53:1: Shemu'athenu can mean "our report" or "what was heard by us." The Hebrew puts "the arm of the LORD" first in its clause, and that order is kept.
native_notes.53:2: Lowercase pronouns are used for the servant and capitals for the LORD ("before Him"). The Hebrew does not mark the servant as divine, and the case keeps the two referents apart in verses such as 53:10. The clause break after "splendor" follows the Masoretic athnach accent under hadar.
native_notes.53:3: Makh'oboth and choli mean "pains" and "sickness"; they are rendered the same way in 53:4. Chadal ishim is literally "ceasing from / lacking men," that is, abandoned by people. Master panim mimmennu is literally "a hiding of faces from him."
native_notes.53:5: Mecholal means "pierced" or "wounded"; the preposition min here means "because of." Musar is discipline or chastening. Nirpa-lanu is an impersonal passive: "it is healed for us," so "healing has come to us." Chavurah is a welt or bruise from blows.
native_notes.53:6: Hifgia bo means "made to meet / strike against him"; "made ... land on him" keeps the image of a burden falling on him. The same verb appears in 53:12, where it means "intercede."
native_notes.53:7: Niggas means "oppressed" or "hard pressed"; na'aneh is passive ("afflicted") but may be reflexive ("he let himself be afflicted"). The repeated imperfect lo yiftach is rendered "would not open" to bring out that he chose silence.
native_notes.53:8: This verse is difficult. Me'otser umimmishpat may mean "by oppression and judgment" or "without restraint and without justice." Doro ("his generation") may mean his contemporaries or his descendants, and yesocheach means "consider" or "complain." Lamo is literally "to them" (or a poetic "to him"); "on him" follows the sense required by the context. The Hebrew has "my people," spoken by the prophet or the LORD.
native_notes.53:9: Wayyitten is impersonal, "one gave," rendered "they assigned." Bemothaw is a plural, "in his deaths," which may be intensive (a violent death) or may mean "his tomb"; the Hebrew plural is kept.
native_notes.53:10: Hecheli is "He made (him) sick," from the same root as choli in 53:3–4. Tasim is either third person feminine with nafsho ("his soul") as subject ("if his soul makes a guilt offering," followed here) or second person addressed to the LORD ("if You make his soul a guilt offering"). Asham is the guilt (reparation) offering of Lev 5.
native_notes.53:11: The Masoretic Text has "he will see" with no object; the Qumran scroll 1QIsa-a and the Septuagint add "light." Since this column translates only the Hebrew, "light" is not supplied. Yatsdiq tsaddiq is a wordplay: "the righteous one will make righteous." Beda'to can mean "by his knowledge" or "by knowing him."
native_notes.53:12: He'erah means "laid bare" or "poured out" (Gen 24:20). Yafgia is the verb of 53:6, here meaning to intercede or intervene.
native_notes.54:5: Both בֹעֲלַיִךְ ('your husband') and עֹשַׂיִךְ ('your Maker') are masculine plural Qal participles used as plurals of majesty referring to the one God (compare Job 35:10; Ps 149:2).
native_notes.54:8: Hebrew בְּשֶׁצֶף קֶצֶף pairs the hapax legomenon שֶׁצֶף ('surge, outburst, flood,' related to שׁטף) with the rhyming noun קֶצֶף ('anger, wrath') for rhetorical emphasis.
native_notes.54:9: The Masoretic Text divides כִּי־מֵי נֹחַ as two words ('for ... the waters of Noah,' matching מֵי־נֹחַ later in the verse), whereas some manuscripts and ancient versions divide it as כִּימֵי נֹחַ ('like the days of Noah').
native_notes.54:15: Hebrew גּוֹר יָגוּר (Qal infinitive absolute plus imperfect 3ms of גור III, 'stir up strife, attack') expresses emphatic attack; אֶפֶס מֵאוֹתִי ('not from Me') uses the rare spelling מֵאוֹתִי for מֵאִתִּי (compare v. 17).
native_notes.54:16: Ketiv reads הן (הֵן, 'look, see'); the Qere הִנֵּה ('look, see,' rendered 'See') carries the same deictic force.
native_notes.55:1: Hebrew hoy here functions as an urgent call of summons rather than a lament of woe, and shivru (Qal imperative of shavar II) specifically means to purchase grain or provisions.
native_notes.55:3: Hebrew chasdei Dawid hanne'emanim (literally 'the proven/sure acts of loyal love of David') uses the Niphal participle of aman in apposition to 'eternal covenant,' referring to the enduring acts of loyal love promised to David.
native_notes.55:13: Translates the Qere 'and instead of' (wetachat); the Ketiv (tachat) lacks the conjunction. The noun sirpad occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes a prickly weed such as a brier or nettle.
native_notes.56:5: Hebrew yad literally means 'hand' and idiomatically denotes a memorial monument or standing place. The final clause shifts in the Masoretic Text to the distributive singular lo (literally 'to him'), rendered 'each one.'
native_notes.56:10: Hebrew hozim (Qal participle of hazah) occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes dreaming or drowsing incoherently. Masoretic tzofaw is a defective spelling of tzofayw ('his watchmen,' referring to Israel).
native_notes.56:11: Hebrew miqqatzehu literally means 'from its end/extremity,' an idiom denoting totality ('without exception').
native_notes.56:12: "They say" is supplied to introduce the abrupt Hebrew quotation, and the closing phrase literally reads "great, exceedingly much."
native_notes.57:3: Hebrew mena'ef wattizneh literally pairs a masculine Piel participle ('an adulterer') with a third-person feminine singular waw-consecutive Qal imperfect verb ('and she commits prostitution'), continuing the construct phrase idiomatically.
native_notes.57:6: Hebrew challaqei-nachal chelqekh creates a wordplay between chalaq ('smooth [stones]') and cheleq ('portion').
native_notes.57:8: Hebrew yad literally means 'hand' and is used here as a euphemism for male nakedness (or possibly a pagan monument/sign, cf. 56:5).
native_notes.57:13: Hebrew qibbutzayikh (a plural noun occurring only here, from qavatz 'gather') literally means 'your gatherings/collections,' an ironic reference to Judah's assembled idols or foreign allies.
native_notes.57:19: Translates the Qere niv ('fruit/produce') rather than the Ketiv nov, an alternate spelling of the same noun.
native_notes.58:8: The Qal verb ya'asfekha (from asaf, "gather") is used idiomatically for gathering in stragglers or serving as a military rear guard.
native_notes.58:10: The Masoretic Text reads nafshekha ("your soul"), idiomatically expressing offering oneself or what one's own appetite desires to the hungry.
native_notes.58:13: The privative sense of turning back from the Sabbath carries over to the infinitive asot ("from doing"); the concluding idiom dabber davar (lit. "speaking a word") denotes everyday talk or business chatter.
native_notes.58:14: Ketiv bmvty (plene spelling with waw) vs. Qere bamotei (construct vocalization without waw); both denote "the heights of" or "high places of."
native_notes.59:3: The verb nego'alu ("are defiled", from ga'al II) is a rare mixed form blending the Niphal prefix with a Pual vowel pattern.
native_notes.59:10: The noun ashmannim is a hapax legomenon of uncertain meaning, here derived from the root shaman ("stout, vigorous") to yield "among the vigorous."
native_notes.59:18: The rare double preposition ke'al ... ke'al ("according to ... accordingly") pairs with a wordplay between gemulot ("deeds") and gemul ("recompense").
native_notes.59:19: Taking tsar as "pent-up" and nosesah as the Polel of nus ("drive forward") yields a river driven by the LORD's breath; an alternative parsing takes tsar as "an adversary" whom the Spirit of the LORD drives back or raises a banner against.
native_notes.60:7: In ya'alu al-ratson mizbechi, the preposition al governs ratson ("with acceptance"), while mizbechi ("onto My altar") functions as an adverbial accusative of destination.
native_notes.60:11: The verb ufittechu is vocalized as an intransitive Piel ("stand open") rather than a passive Pual, emphasizing that the gates remain continuously open.
native_notes.60:19: Unlike the Septuagint, the Masoretic Text does not include "by night" in the second clause; the translation follows the MT strictly.
native_notes.60:21: Ketiv mt'v ("His planting", 3ms singular) vs. Qere matta'ai ("My plantings", 1cs plural); the Qere is translated, aligning with 1cs "My hands" in the next clause.
native_notes.61:1: The rare reduplicated noun peqach-qoach, translated 'freedom,' derives from the root paqach ('to open,' usually of eyes) and literally means a 'wide opening,' pointing to the opening of the prison or release from dungeon darkness into light.
native_notes.61:3: The Hebrew employs wordplay between pe'er ('headdress') and epher ('ashes'), and concludes with the Hithpael infinitive lehithpa'er ('to glorify Himself' or 'display His splendor') from the same root as 'headdress.'
native_notes.61:6: The rare Hithpael verb tithyammaru ('you will boast') is usually derived from a by-form of amar ('to boast, exalt oneself'), though some derive it from mur ('to exchange,' i.e., succeed to their glory).
native_notes.61:8: The Masoretic pointing be'olah literally reads 'in a burnt offering' (rejecting stolen goods offered to God), though the same consonants can represent a contracted spelling of 'awlah, 'wrongdoing' or 'injustice.'
native_notes.61:10: The verb yekahen ('puts on... like a priest') is the Piel of kahan, normally 'to serve as a priest,' here paired with pe'er ('headdress') to evoke a priest's ceremonial turban (cf. 61:3, 6).
native_notes.62:3: Following the qere tseniph ('turban' or 'diadem'); the written ketiv reads tsenoph, a variant noun form with the same meaning.
native_notes.62:4: The symbolic names 'My Delight Is in Her' (Hebrew Hephzibah) and 'Married' (Hebrew Beulah) play directly on the verbs chaphets ('delights') and tiba'el ('will be married') at the end of the verse.
native_notes.62:5: The Masoretic text reads banayikh ('your sons'), picturing the restored inhabitants taking Zion as a bride; the same Hebrew consonants without vowels could also be vocalized bonayikh ('your Builder').
native_notes.63:3: The verb eg'alti ('I stained') is an Aramaizing Hiphil perfect form of ga'al II ('to stain, defile'), creating wordplay with ge'ulay ('My redemption,' from ga'al I) in v. 4. The noun netsach ('lifeblood') denotes spurting juice or blood.
native_notes.63:9: Following the qere lo ('to Him'), forming the Hebrew idiom 'He was distressed' (literally 'it was distressing to Him'); the written ketiv reads lo' ('not').
native_notes.63:11: The Masoretic text has the compressed clause 'remembered the days of old, Moses, His people,' here smoothed with 'His people' as subject, and reads the plural ro'ey ('shepherds of His flock,' e.g., Moses and Aaron).
native_notes.63:14: The Masoretic verb tenichennu is the Hiphil of nuach ('granted them rest,' literally 'gave it rest,' referring collectively to the people), rather than nachah ('led').
native_notes.63:19: In the Masoretic verse division the plea 'If only You would tear open the heavens...' belongs to 63:19, and chapter 64 begins with the next verse. The verb nazollu is the Niphal of zalal ('to quake').
native_notes.64:1: This verse continues the theophany plea of 63:19, whose second half begins the plea in the Masoretic division. The noun hamasim ("brushwood") is a hapax legomenon denoting dry twigs or kindling.
native_notes.64:2: The verb nazollu ("quaked") is pointed as a Niphal perfect of zll II ("shake, quake"), matching 63:19, though its sound also evokes nzl ("flow, melt").
native_notes.64:4: The closing clause bahem olam weniwwashea ("in them we have been a long time, and shall we be saved?") is sharply elliptic in the Masoretic Text; "in them" is usually taken to refer to the sins just confessed, with a verb of continuance understood before the Niphal niwwashea.
native_notes.64:6: The Masoretic form wattemugenu is a transitive Qal wayyiqtol of mwg ("melt, dissolve"), whereas ancient versions such as the Septuagint and Syriac reflect the root mgn ("deliver up").
native_notes.65:1: The Masoretic vocalization qora is a Pual perfect passive ("was not called by My name"), rather than the Qal active qara ("did not call on My name") reflected in the Septuagint and Vulgate.
native_notes.65:4: Ketiv/Qere: the Ketiv reads wprq ("piece" or "broth"), while the Qere followed here reads umeraq ("and broth of").
native_notes.65:5: The Qal perfect with direct object suffix qedashtika ("I am holier than you") uses a comparative construction, or may express infectious taboo holiness ("I would transmit holiness to you" by contact).
native_notes.65:7: Ketiv/Qere: the Ketiv reads al ("upon"), while the Qere followed here reads el ("into their lap"), contrasting slightly with al-heqam ("onto their lap") in 65:6.
native_notes.65:11: "Fortune" and "Destiny" translate the definite divine names ha-Gad and ha-Meni; the latter creates a wordplay with umaniti ("I will destine," from mnh) at the beginning of 65:12.
native_notes.66:3: The four opening clauses use terse verbless juxtapositions without a comparative particle (literally "one who slaughters an ox—one who strikes down a man"), equating hypocritical sacrifices with pagan abominations; awen ("idol") literally means "iniquity" or "wickedness."
native_notes.66:11: The verb tamotzu ("drink deeply," Qal of mtz) is a hapax legomenon, and the rare noun ziz ("abundance") is cognate with Akkadian zizu ("teat, breast"), paralleling shod ("breast") in the first half of the verse.
native_notes.66:17: Ketiv/Qere: the Ketiv reads the masculine ehad ("one"), while the Qere followed here reads the feminine ahat ("one"), likely referring to a female cult leader or goddess figure in the center of the garden rite.
native_notes.66:18: The opening clause we'anoki ma'asehem umahshevotehem ba'ah is highly elliptic in the Masoretic Text, omitting a finite verb after "And I" (supplied as "know") and using the feminine singular Qal participle ba'ah impersonally for "the time is coming."
native_notes.66:20: The noun kirkarot ("dromedaries") is a hapax legomenon denoting swift riding camels, and tzabbim ("covered wagons") matches Numbers 7:3.
